Mr. S. Brighouse, Coroner for-So-u-th---w-e; Lanca- shire, held an inquiry at the White Hart Hotel, Sankey-st., Warrington, on Monday afternoon, into the circumstances of the death of John Broadhurst (6.2), who wito thrown from a cart and killed while ;in Cockhedge-lane, on Friday in last week, under ' }circumstances that have been previously reported. -Sarah Ann Harding, wife of James Harding, of; 20 Napier-st. said that she was a daughter of the ' deceased, who lived with her. Deceased was 62 years of age. He was a painter by trade, but latterly he had earned a livelihood by selling pota- toes and grtengroceries, which he took about ins cart. She last saw the deceased alive at about eleven o'clock on Friday morning, when lie left the , house with the horse and cart. He was then well, and in good health. At noon she heard that lie had fallen out of the cart, and went to Cockhedge-lane, where she saw the deceased being lifted into a cab. Deceased was sober when he left home.-Clara Letitia Lythgoe, of 44 James-st., deposed that on Friday morning she was turning the corner of ' Naylor-at., going into Cock licslge-lane, at about noon, when she saw the deceased in his cart, sat on two ! I hampers. There was a stone at the corner, in I Cockliedge-lane, dividing the corner of the shop from the lane. Witness saw the deceased fall from !the cart to the ground alighting on his head. ' The cart was near the stone when he fell out, but witness did not see if the wheel came in contact with the stone, She was too far away. The deceased lay where he Inland did not move, and the cart that ne had been driving passed an.— Elizabeth Naylor, wife of Henry Naylor, Di James- street, said that an Friday she heard people scream lug, and was told tufa a man had fallen from a cart. She went to the place and saw the deceased who appeared to be dead. A cab was sent for, and deceased was taken to the Infirmary in it. The lane was very narrow, but conveyances and tarries went through.-If • lurry was in the Street passengers bad to wait until it had gone past. - The Coroner said that he had been informed by the police that the road, at the place where the acci- dent occurred, was only four feet and eleven inchea wide, and that the parapet, where there was one, was two feet wide. To get down the street carte had to pass over the parapet.- Several of the jurymen said that they considered that the road wasltlangerous, and the Coroner sougested that it might be advisable to draw the attention of the Corporation to the matter, and ask them to deal with it. -A Juryman But if they don't. The Coroner: You must turn out your representatives in the Town Council at the next electi on.-The Jury returned a verdict of accidental death, but added the following presentment ---"Tire jurors present that Cockhedge-lane, in its pr,sent con- dition, lad angeroun to those travelling along it, and that the attention of the Corporation be drawn to the state of the same with a view to its improve m ent."

PRESENTATION TO AN IRON WORKER AT WARRINGTON. On Saturday evening the mill men employed on the Bewsey side of Messrs. Pearson, Knowles, and Co.'s Works made a presentation of a beautiful timepiece, to Mr. Jevins, with whom they had worked and who is leaving Warrington. The presentation took place at the house of Mrs. Butterworth, the Central Hotel, but previous to the ceremony a sumptuous repast was partaken of by the company assembled, over sixty in number, amongst whom were Messrs. J. Bissell, It. Smith. J.. Ashton, O. Yates, T. Tucker, G. Morrall,E Morrell, J. Salt, T. Critchley, J. Baker, 11. Whitehouse, 0, Gough, G. Mom, W. Wilkinson, W. Baker, J. Houghton. T. Pys, J. Worley, Jevins. J. Potter, &c. Mr. J. Podmore, of Blackpool, made an efficient carver, and attended well to the wants of his guests. On the removal of the cloth Mr. Salt was appointed chairman, on the proposition of Mr. R. Smith, seconded by Mr. Bissell. The Chairman said he could not let the opportunity pass without express- ing the regret at the removal of Mr. Jevine from amongst thorn, for be had endeared himself to them all, as was shown by the spontaneous manner in which they had contnbuted to the testimonial , about to be presented to Lim. It must be highly pleasing, he was sure, to Mr. Jevins to hear this, but he could assure him such was the fact, and general regret was felt when it was first known that he intended to leave Warrington. (Applause.) Mr. Ilissam. then made the presentation. It had, he said, been iirrangeil that the presentation should be made by Mr. Wakefield, but illness had prevented bins being with them that evening. Ile reeve,„ tted this, as he was sure they ail would—three, hearl—for Mr. Wake- field having had perhaps mere to do with Mr. Jevim in his everyday work, and knowing more of him, was undoubtedly the moat proper person to make the pre- sentation. He was glad they had not allowed Mr. Jevins to leave them without letting bins know the estimation in which he was held, for lie had proved I self a most •st sad' worker. It '

' Art Gallery, affords a special opportunity to those who know how to feast their eyes. It is to be hoped, as a correspondent suggests, that the loan I will not be the last of its kind. There are few ! picture collectors who are so selfish us to wish to keep what they have to themselves : they are as rule above the dog-in-the-manger feeling,and have, only to be assured that their treasures will be , eared for and appreciated to be induced to part with them for a time. Mr. Barlow,the Warrington manager of the Manchester and County Bank. I might, for instance, he solicited to lend his admir- I able collection of paintings and drawings ; and advantage might he taken of the fact that Mr, John Platt. LP., is about to remove from Walton to induce him for a brief space to adorn the walls of the Warrington Gallery with his choice works of art. Hut we are getting away from Mr. Green- wood's book which, it should be added, treats of everything relating to Museums and Art Galleries --such matters for instance, as their relation to the State : their place in education : private aid ; , Sunday opening elssaification of objects; hints on management ; museum lectures, Ac. Mr. , Greenwood has done well; he has produced a much-needed work; and presented it in a style ! which is alike practical and popular.

The arbitration proceedings to 118StF5 the com- pensation due to Sir GILBERT GIMENALL for the land belonging to him which is required for the imrposee of the Ship Canal, have excited not a little interest in Warrington and the neighbour- hood. There are people who say that the member for Warrington might to have been glad to give the forty-one acres required; as, when the Canal is made, he will, in all probability, get the value back many times over. But he does not look at things in that way ; he likes his pound of flesh, and will ' have everything that is nominated in the bond. , He is entitled of course to all he can get, but hav- ing extracted the uttermost farthing, it is to be hoped we shall hear no more, at election times, about the way in which the lord of the Manor of Walton has aided the Ship Canal Company. Per- haps Sir GILBERT has been egged on by valuers' they are certainly an interesting body of men. How beautifully they can clap it on when it suits their purpose ! And how well it all sounds till; you hear the other side ! The Arbitrator must have a lively time of it if he is a laughing philoso- pher. One set of valuers proceeds to demonstrate toafarthing that Sir GILBERT GRRENALLiS entitled to over t MOM; whilst the other shows quite as oonclusively that he would be well compensated with just half that earn.

elicited the startling statement that when Mr. Wean: was before a Parliamentary Committee, in 1884, he named £12.5 per acre as the value of Sta GILBERT'S land. Mr. Worm explains that his valuation at that time was a joint valuation with Mr. DUNLOP, and that he did not then know sthat the member for Warrington had paid for the land. But the question is not what a wealthy brewer may have paid to build , up an estate, but what the land is really worth. In any case, it does not add to Mr. Warren's reputation that there should be Doi great a difference between the figures laid before the Parliamentary Committee and those laid before tho Arbitrator. As to the suggestion that the value of land has recently increased in the neigh- bourhood of Stockton Heath and Latchford, we should say that, if this be no, it is mainly because of improved proepecta through the making of the Ship Canal. It is surely hard on the Ship Canal Company that they should he compelled to pay an increased price for the land they require becalm°, by requiring it fern great improvement, they have iadded to the value of all the land in the district. Then, too. as following upon this, claims for cent- ponaation for damages are altogether peculiar, !except, of course, in specific and obvious cam.. Speaking generally, we are inclined to agree with Mr. Alderman Scrrox (Mayor of Warrington), who, when called ants witness, said "if he were the owner .if land in that locality, he should be disposed to consider that a canal go- ing through it would be a benefit to him more than anything else." Mr. Sarrox's total valuation, it should be noted, amounted to £B,lOB as against the "grand total" of £17,708 12s. which was put in by Mr. Joni( Wmrs. It is not for no of course to say whore i the truth lien: that is a matter for the Arbitrator, who is fully competent to deal with it; but, look- ing at the enormous disparity in the evidence adduced at the inquiry, we realise the force of the epigram of the brilliant Queen's Counsel who : said: " There are three classes of liars; there is , the liar ; the—liar, and the skilled witness."

SATURDAY, JANUARY 19, 1889.

Mr. THOMAS GREENWOOD, F.G.S., did the State some service when he published his work on Free Public Libraries, for previous to its issue there was no comprehensive work on. the subject. He brought to his task patience,akill, and enthusiasm, and produced a book winch isexceedingly readable as well as solid and useful. There can be no ques- tion that it excited interest, and that it led many local authorities to look up the question of estab- lishing a Free Library. Thbilmikingup has resulted in some cases in the Piddle Libraries Act being adopted, awl this HICSOS that various communities I have b,ome pc.nbuiently henalitcd. Mr. GREEN- I wool, Lis done good 'mirk, lint, happily, his good work is nit donc. He has just issued a goodly mixed %alone - a kindred work --with the title of Museunm and Art Galleries." It is pub- I tithed by Messrs. Sill KIN MA ROL% M. and CO,l 4iondon, and, like its predecessor, it boars every evidence, not only 11 thoroughness, but of being a labour of hive. Mr. I iRIIENWOOII is zealous toner in the field he has chosen ; he is a missionary in fact. He believes he is on the right track ;he desires others to follow him; and it is because we have strong sympathy with him that we call special attention to " Museums and Art Galleries." The book is one which ought, certainly, to be in the hands of all who aspire to a higher and better order of things in municipal government. Main does not live by bread alone ; he has wants which are not wholly met when; the streets are cowered, and paved, and lighted, and when there is a publican and a policeman at every corner. There is a hunger and thirst of mind as well as of body, and just in proportion as men became civilized do they recognize the fact, and provide accordingly. It is a great and goo.] thing to etstablish a Free Library ; and it is all the ; LAWr when to the Library there are added is Museum and Art Gallery. It is tint easy to main- tain and feed these three institutions out of the rste if one penny in the pound, to which municipalities are at present I ted; and relies Parliament gets time to do its duty in this matter it will free grown-up people from these leading strings. -

Meantime;he Act leaves plenty of wipe for the exercise of private munificence ; and it is satis- factory to We that, in some parts of the country, 'there has heen mothing wanting in this respect. A perusal of Mr. GREENWIIOO"S hook would he useful to the rich nien Who are laying up treasures on earth, and hardly know what to do with then,. div.head: RUNCORN V. BRADFORD.
div.p: RUNCORN V. BRADFORD.

(Runcorn 3 goals, 3 tries, 5 minors; Bradford 1 minor) Brave Noncom's t ,the fore, boys, With all its inborn pluck ; We trust to skill and daring, boys, And not to chance or luck. Wbene'er we fight, we fight, boys, The goal we mean to gain ; We strove and won the day, boys, And so we can again.

The Bradford boys came boasting Of fame and wide renown ; We lowered their Mors just a bit To keep the bunkum down. When next they come to meet us, We surely can maintain That Cheshire lads beat Yorkshire, And so they can again. And so we can fr.c.

We kept the leather moving. And o'er their line we pressed ; We kept them in their Quarter, boys, Despite their level best. We tackled, pase,d, and dribbled ; Their toil was all in vain ; Thegoal three times we cleared, boys, And so we can again. And so we can he.
Then let us on our banner Inscribe in line of flaw, That" deeds not words "are needed, boys,
. Let's then press boldly forward, Look well to field and melt ; We won the day before, boys. And so we can again. And so we can Ste., du.

'January 12th, 1889 W. H. WARVINGTON V. MANCHE...III Rawness" A" TEAMS.— The above teams met on the Wildempool ground on Saturday last, before a moderate number of spectators. , Two thirties were arranged, and Adamson, wanting the ' toss, decided ta play with the wind in Ins favour. After souse gem and take play, Donoghue picked up and passed to Holmes who eluded his opponents nicely and gamed a brilliant try, which Warburton converted into a goal. I Vickers restarted, but through some of the players being offside, a pack was formed in midfield, from when. Lawless secured and passed to Speakman, who put in a goal punt, carrying play to the Rangers' territory. A nice bit of passing was fiere witnessed between the home backs, Bibby putting in a goal kick. A pack was formed close to the Rangers' posts, eventually forcing Hill to concedes minor. Speakman replied to the drop out by kicking into touch in the visitors' 25. From the line-out the Rangers took play to centre, anti Bosco pick- ing up. put ins nice kick, causing play to rage near the Rangers' hoe, where it was confined principally for some length of time. The visitors obtained a free kick for an ' infringement, and Warburton getting bold took a drop , at goal, a dead ball resulting. The drop out brought the visitors no rdief, the ball metering touch in their 25. From the park lawless secured and, running round his opoinents,got over the line close to the corner flag, Isher- wood failing at the place kick. Fortune dropped out, the oval going into touch in centre. Daniels was next conspicuous 11 a good run across the fidd but unfortu- nately kicked irco touch. Donoghue, Holmes, and Isher- wood broke away from the line out, carrying play to the Rangers' 25. Lawless here secured and passed to Daniels who ran over the line, but was ruled back for some previous informality. Half thne was called, the score standing Warring en 1-1-2 to Rangers nothing. Bosom. ing at half may, Isherwood kicked off, and no return boing made, play raged in the Rangers' territory, Mather was prominent with anise run, and in transit passed %Daniels, who put in a kick to the Rangers' quarters. The home backs indulged in some pretty passing, Phelan foiling Speakman by taking his pao, but Bosce picked up and punted into touch. The visitors took play to ryntre, Bibby saving. From a line-out Beard, Adamson, and Molyneux beaded a dribble tip the field. Hill sayingby a flying kick into touch. Play rested for a short period in the home half, and a succession of scrimmages enabled the tome main to gain a little ground. Promo line-out Battey got the oval away, but spoilt a splendid opportunity by kicking dead. No reply being made t.; the dmp out, play rested in the Ranger's territory, where from a pack the home torwards broke away. Hill securing kicked to Bosco, who returned into touch. From a line-out 1.. Holmes obtained possossion and made a grand run and, i dodging his opponents in a brilliant manner, gained his second try. Warburton kicking a goal. Speakman replied to the kiek of, the ball rolling into touch.

IVIOXES ST. MART M T. 4TM L.A.V.—This match which was to he played at Wavertree, on Saturday, was cancelled by Widnes an account of not being able to , furnish a team when the time arrived. MEIMET CON'. WORKS V. Ithonsnam.—A match between the above teams was played on the Widnes ground, on Saturday. The visitors proved the superior, and play eventually ended with a one-sided score Pmdsham, 1 goal, 3 tam; Widnes Copper Works, 2 minors. This heavy score may in some respect be accounted for, as the Frodsham men came to Widnes with only nine men, and the root -were made up from the West Rank Rangers, who hart no fixtures. At half- time the score was—Frixlsham, 1 goal and 1 try; Copper Works, 1 minor. The Rangers got all the tries. Wm.. V. CROMVTION.—The Widnes team journeyed to Crompton, on Saturday, hut were without the assist- ance of Ilumpton, Farrell, and Hardman. The home HIM put their strongest team on the field, but for a con- siderable wart of the game the visitors played one man Moot. The utmost interest was thrown into the contest, and throughout the game play was very fast and excit- ing. A few minors were scored in the first half, but it was only in the second part that any tangible point was gained. Roth teams attacked alternately, and pleasant play was witnessed bs• a large number of spectators. Stott succeeded in dishing over the coveted mark , between the posts and gained the first try., while Walsh's place-kick proved a niece" the major wont being added amid some applause. At the close. Crompton were declared winders by one goal and Ave minors to Widnes three minors. .

..... BRADFOUD a. RUNIMPIOI. Played at Runcorn, a bitterly cold wind blowing down the field, but the 'surf was in a dry and favourable state for a fast game. A large crowd had assembled to witcesa the game, numbers of spectators' having travelled from Warring- ton and Widnes. On the teams entering the field it was noted that E. Wilkinson and J. Patter were the only players on the Bradford side who helped to defeat : Runcorn early on in the season at Park Avenue. Wilkinson winning the teat. H. WARRINGTON V. MANCHESTER RANGERS.

This interesting fixture was decided at Itusholme ott Saturday, only a moderate number of spectators witness- ing the match. The Warringtonians were only poorly , represented,Fair Turner, Antrohus, and Barnes (who had not thoroughly recovered from the effects of a sprained ankle received whilst practising at the Gymnasium a few evenings ago) being absent. The visitors made the journey with only 14 men, hut luckily Evans journeyed on a slow train, reaching the scene on the point of kicking off. The Rangers, on the other hand, mustensl a capital team, and as it had never been the good fortune of the Manchester men to lower the colours of the wirepullers," their prospects on the present occasion Iss-ed very favourable.

Frank Turner started operations, the anal going in touch at the Rangers' 25. Bate got away from the first pack formed, and almost scored in the first minute, but his pass was mulled. Median responded with a tall punt to the half-way Rag, but neat passel by the 1 Warrington halves placed the Rangers on is defensive , attitude, and a rush, headed by Littlewoo.l and Dillon, ' took the leather over the line, one of the visitors ground- ing, but only a minor was awarded. Jolley net the drop-out in excellent style, and his efforts were seconded by Evans, whose kick woo well followed up by the Warrington forwards, no reply being effected. Jolley : almost got in soon after, and Gadd wa.s commented to concede a minor, the outcome of a long kick by Speak- man. Now the homesters showed up with -renewed , vigour, for Pollard and Harry Hasleham put in a spirited rush, but a run by Paterson was nipped in the bud by Massey. Jolley stopped ltateliffe's career, and a : well directed pass from Speakman to Evans allowed the! latter once more to place the game at the Rangers' , quarter flag. A free kick to the Manchester Wain was of no avail, but J. Jolley pluckily saved after Isis kick had been charged down. Mealsan tried to effect an opening, but all to no purpose, for the tackling was too sure. Warrington still continued to harass the Rangers' defence, but all efforts to cross their line proved fruitless, and halftime was called with the I score—Warrington, 0-4-2; Rangers, 0-0-1. If. ' Haaleham restarted, and for a time play was confined to neutral ground. However, a well-combined rush of the' visiting forwards from half-vray, foremost amongst I others being Ashurst,fffillon' and Ashton, took theleather over the line, and Handles being in attendance, cons- pletcd the try, Frank Turner failing to augment the 1 point. A drop at goal by Evans forced another minor, I and Sixes after the drop-out the Rangers rushed the oval I down the field, Massey putting a stop to their progress by a3udicious kick into touch. Not to be denied, the home team still pressed, and for a while it looked a.s if ' their efforts would meet with mimosa. The danger was only momentary, and good passing by tho Warrington backs placed the issue beyond doubt. From now Is, the call of time the visitors kept up an aggressive attitude. Individual efforts by Evans and Bate are deserving of notice, and kindles ought to have got in again from a , rush of his forwards. T Jolley got in a tremendous kick from the half-way flag, and although Hammett and Meahan tried hard to relieve, it was all to no purpose, I , and when the whistle had sounded" no side,' Warring- ton retired vicmrs by one try, four minors, totwo minors. Commenting on the garnet the score does not in any way represent the true merits of the two teams. For fully three parts of the match the game was contested : in the Rangers quartem' but luck was sadly against the , Warringtonlans no regards scoring. Two points that were specially noticeable were the unproved form shown I:llelkol;ntfte7ndatcral s'itnglic°lni°i'stieTe up. urrerPil the tackling line. T. Jolley had little work to do, hut accomplished it in a satisfactory manner. The three- quarters were very safe, whilst Bate made an excellent suhltitute for Antrobus, Speakman showed all his old dash, whilst lathe forward departments Dillon, Ashton, Littlewood, aud Povey deserve special notice for their efforts. Tbe time appointed for the commencement of the game was three o'clock, but long before that time a con- stant stream of intending spectators passed over the bridge and along Wilderspoot Causeway to the field of play. 'The square arena in which die footballers are wont to disport themselves was soon surrounded on all sides by a dense crowd, which seemed at some parts to be five or six deep, while the rapacious grandstand was clusely packed. Thee crowd wm by no means entirely composed of local admirers of the game, for, the rail- way companies having offered special faciliti., a fair proporteon of the on-lookers had travelled lir= neighbouring towns--St. Helens, Runcorn, 1 ; Widnes and Wigan all being represented. The Warring., ltoss team, headed by their captain, W. Dillon, in his county jersey, were the first to put in an appearance,and they were gieeted with an encouraging cheer. A few minutes later the Maoris emerged (menthe Pavilion and ;they were the recipients of a very cordial greeting, the ' amilause being snare than usually enthusiastic. Their ' fine physique was atone,' the subject of comment and admiration. Several of them were of more than the, usual height, and all seemed proportioned for strengthl land agility. Their appearance, solar as mere smartness was concerned, wan rather detractal Mona by the rather :1 dirty condition of their to, costumes, winch bore '7.7ry perceptible trews of previous e,nflicts on damp I.noel muddy grounds. The teams as they (seed each other, the Maoris defending the goal on the railway side, ' were composed as follows . klamus.—Full back, W. Warbrck ; three-quarter back, McCausland, Wynyard, Madigan; half backs, Elliot, Keogh, Gage; forwards, Taiarva, Williams, Rene, Stewart Ellison Lee S. Wynward and Kauraria

There was an intense silenee amongst the spectators as Ellison not the ball in motion for the visitow, and Evans made a capital return to half-way. Handlm at once ran the ball well into the Maori quarter, but aluest in a mrment the tatters forwards, gathering themselves into a compact body, broke through the opposing players, and, keeping the oval at their to., were down to the Warrington quarter flag in wonderfully quick time, Evans being collared no he attempt rd to save, and the Maoris by really splendid passing from one to another completely overcame the home ; defence, and W. Winyard was over the line within two urinates of the start. 1 Vinyard, however, did not ground till he was over the play line, awl had even touched the fence. The validity of the try was therefore strongly disputed lw the local players, but was allowed by Mr. Crooks, the referee, on; the ground that i it had not been explained to the visitors that passing the line took the ball out of play. It is probable. however, I that this try, from which MeCamland kicked a goal, will be the subject of further appeal. The Maoris had now displayed some of their qualities. The impetus, and even headlong rush of the forwards woo in the time place the means of their securing this first point, and in the second place it NV:49 due to remarkable quick and accurate passing while going along at almost. full spood. ,1 This fine pawing may indeed be said to have been the ' best feature in the Maori play. The boil was trans- ferred with great quickn.s and the player to whom it was thrown scarcely ever nrissed laying hold. Instead of being disheartened by this early reverse, Warrington played air with greater vigour than ever, , and almost throughout tire rest of the first half they taxed the Maori defence to the utmost. Nevirra by a fine run very nearly approached the opposing line, and had Ilia pass been taken smartly Warrington would almost inevitably have scored. Severe scrimmaging followed, in which there was some rough offside play by , the visitors. Antrobus secured from one of these scrim- mages, and by a tine dodgy run all but got over. The visitors at length found relief in a long run by Winyard, who worst length brought down near the Warrington line by Jolley. The home forwanis again put on the screw no severely tha, the Maoris were fortunate in being able to concede a touch-down after a severe maul. Still the wirepullers pressed, and another maul took place over the line, a scrimmage being ordered, and soon after another minor had lobe conceded lw the Maoris. Half- time came with Ore ball within the Maoris twenty-five, the score bring, Maoris one goal, Warrington two I minors.

---The game was re-started by Frank Turner, and War- rington soon took the advantage by their forward play. A capital rim by Winyard threatened danger, but he was brought down by Evans in the nick of time. Soon after Winyard was again to the fore, taking a pant by Elliott and cantering over the line ton fine position, McCausland scoring the premier point. Warrington still played up, with unabated pluck, notwitlstanding their reyerses, but much time hail not elapsed before , Elliott was over the line, but the ball was ruled back on account of an informality. Elliott, however, again secured from Keogh, and, racing up to near the line, made a pass to Winyard, who was in elase attendance and the latter again got over, McCausland failing in his kick at a difficult place. Things now began to look black for the home team, but the latter refused to acknowledge defeat, and played with as MUCh energy as ever, and this spirited conduct was at length rewarded by Nevins struggling over at the quarter-2v. Fair. Turner failed tO notch the premier point from a difficult place. Tie rest of the play was net eventful, and the game ended as follows: "nuts tnt. 1 1 2

, In COlnmenting on the play it cannot but he admitted , that the game was not near so one-sided as the wore would indicate. Warrington were extremely unfortun- ate, especially in the first half, when, although they penned their opponents near their line, they were unable 'to score a tangible point. The home forwuds never : showed to letter advantage, but the three-quarters seemed rather weak in comparison with their opponents. The play of the half backs was considerably marred by the over eager play of MiWri halves, who seemed to pay little Ivgard to eIY-side niles. On the other hand the Maoris are undoubtedly a most formidable combination. Their speed and strength is much above the average of most teams, anti their accurate passing and sure picking up were generally admired. THE GATE.

In the evening the visitors were entertained by the Warrington Football Club to a dinner at the Con.serva- tire Club. The CNAINNAN, having .I;;;nrioned that the visitors were obliged to leave by the 7.55 train, said he had risen for the purpose of proposing the toast which, he supposed, .they should consider the most important toast, whirl, was tied of their Maori friends. I been on the victorious vote, but he (the chairman) was a sufficiently g..d sportsman to takes good beating by Illan better than hiinielf with a good grace. Their friends came from the other side of the world, as it were, or they might say from the bottom of the world from where they were at that time, and they were all very pleas.l indeed to think that Rugby football had spread, no to speak, to the uttermost parts of the earth. (Rear, hear.) Ile was told by Mr. Winyard that the population of New Zealand WAS only about 600,000, and he thought it was a very great credit to New Zealand that it could tom out a team which could play such a game of football as they had on that day. The toast was drunk very cordially with musical honours, and an amusing song was next given by Mr. Percy Davits.. Mr. MeCarstaxn, in responding to the toast, thanked thorn on behalf of his tarn for the very hearty manner in which the taut had been proposed, and in winch it had been received. They had had a very enjoyable day since they arrived; they had been shown through the various works of the town, and altogether the time had pass., very pleasantly, although thy had unfortunately been a bit late in getting to Warrington. With regard to tiro game he had not very much to say. It was a pleasant game, and very heartily contested. Of course he could not cotnplain of their having been victorious, as they wished to take a few victories home with them to talk about when they got there, yet he did not mind admitting that the wore did not really represent the state of the game, which had been so closely fought that it was almost anybody's game up to the very close. (Dear, hear.) Before he sat down, he would ask the members of the Maori hvm to drink the health of tie ; Warrington Football Club, and wisli them every success in their future matches. He coupled this toast with the name of Mr. W. Dillon, captain of the Warrington team. (Applause.) This toast was duly; henour.l by the members of the visiting team, who saeg tt For they are jolly good fellows," with great heartimws, and concluded with the Maori words, " Ake, ake, kia, kaha," which, it was explained, meant in, Englisn, "May they be for over strong." Mr. W. Ptcr,oN, in responding on behalf of the War rington team, said he was very pleased to see the way in ' which the toast had been drunk. In speaking of the match that day, he quite agreed with the Maori cap- tain in saying that the scent didn't indicate the play. The game itself was a very good one indeed, and it required a good ttwin to boat the Maoris. (hear, hear.) lie was sure that they had with them the wishes of the Warrington team that they might win all their future matches, and that their gates might be even more nume- rous than their previolo ones, and that, when they came to return home, Hwy Might all have a happy and safe journey. div.head: GRAND FOOThALL MATCH. WARRINGTON V. MAORIS.
div.p: GRAND FOOThALL MATCH. WARRINGTON V. MAORIS.

The fixture of the Warrington Football Club with the Maori team, which is at present on a tour in England, was looked forward to with an amount of local interest which was probably unexampled in the football annals of Warrington. This was I undoubtedly very largely due to the very fine record I the Maoris have established. I TIIE MAORIS RECORD IN ENGLAND. Since coming to this country, up to the time of their playing Warrington, on Thursday, they had played 43 matches, 26 of which they had won, lost 13, and drawn 4. This is a particularly good record I when it is considmed that their opponents have ! almost in every instance been leading teams in their respective districts, several of the defeated being strong county combinations. Their first game was at Richmond on October 3rd, when,after a very I fast game, they beat county representatives of Surrey by one goal, one try, three minors, to one try one minor. Northamptonshire county was the next to have to submit to their superior powers by the very decisive score of two goals and four tries to nil. Blackheath having been given the" happy despatch," the New Zealainers met with their first reverse at the hands of Moseley, another Midland combination; Burton-on-Trent soon after inflicting a second defeat by 1-1-7 to 1-0-4. A Midland counties selec- tion were overcome by three goals and a try to nil, , but, on the other hand, the Maoris had next to 1 I submit to a still more decisive reverse when they met a very strong team brought together by Mr. Rowland Hill, secretary of the Rugby Union, the score being 2-3-3 to Maoris nil. Coming north, they were defeated by Hull and Wakefield Trinity, and drew with Northumberland County, but defeated Dewsbury, Stockton-on-Teen, and Tyriemouth. Mali- I fax drubbed them severely by 4-1-9 to 1-1-0, but I after this they won seven successive victories. In; Lancashire, Swinton lowered their colours by a , victory of two tries to nil, but, on the other hand,l they proved superior to Liverpool find District. In a short visit to Ulster they drew with Trinity I College, and defeated North of Ireland. Returning to Lancashire,they played • fairly even genie with the county representatives, though the latter notched a majonty of points, and within a few days , after they overcame what may he called • junior Yorkshire, county team. Breaking the till then inviolate record of Wigan, the Antipodeans next spent a somewhat chequered time in Wales. De- feated by the picked men of the Principality, Llanelly, and Cardiff, they were successful against Newport and Swansea. We next find them in Yorkshire suffering defeat from Bradford, but beat- ing Leeds Parish Church, Kirkstall, and Brighouse Rangers. Last Saturday they drew with Stockport, and early in the week were defeated by Castleford by three goals to three tries. Of the Warrington team it may be mentioned that out of 19 matches played this season they have won 13, lost 3, and drawn 3. TIIE ARRIVAL AT TIIE CENTRAL STATION. . . . .

I The members of the Maori train were expected to I arrive at the Central Station by the train that arrives front Manchester at ten minutes to eleven o'clock in the morning, and by about half•past ten o'clock a crowd began to collect in the vicinity of the elation entrance, . where a conveyance to which were attached four horses j was in waiting. By the time that the train was due to arrive several hundred people had ...doled, and a number of gentlemen wlci take an interest in the doings of the local club went on the platform to give the visitors a welcome ma soon as the train arrived. Amongst them were Councillor H. W. Franeornb, J.C., Mr. John Evans, Mr. Percy Davies, Mr. P. S. Howell, Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, Mr. H. Ashton, Mr.Jamw Smethurst, Mr, C. it. Adamson (captain of the "A" team?, Mr. W. Antro- bus, Mr. T. Barnes, as well as several local footballers. • When the express tame steaming into the station a rush was made to find the saloon in which the visitors were to travel, and some disappointment was felt when it was found that they had not come by that train. It was explained that another train was due to arrive at a few minutes past eleven, but as the Maoris did not come by

div.head: LETTER FROM AIR. JAMES WINSTANLEY.
div.p: LETTER FROM AIR. JAMES WIN- STANLEY.

SALEM, 011.1300 N, Dec. 23rd, Dear Sir,—According to promise I send you a few lines respecting the State in which I have located. If you think them sufficiently interesting ito publish, well and good; if not, there sno offence. Oregon is one of the Western States of the American Republic. It covers MI area of 9600 square miles, and within its limits are to be found some of the highest mountains and fertile valleys in this vast continent. Immense rivers, fed by numerous streams, flow from south to north. Through the entire length, the Cascade range of mountains running, north and south right through , the centre of the State, divides a great portion from the immense plains of Central America, thus pro- tecting it from the blizzards and fierce storms which often rage across some of the States east of the Cascades, while on the west side the mean tem- perature for the winter months is 56 degrees. The summer just past, from July to October, was one succession of cloudless sunshine each afternoon. The breeze from the coast makes the evenings delightful. About the 10th of October, the rains starred—not the cold cutting rains of the old country—but steady showers of warm rain, which is the means of causing vegetiation to spring up a-fresh with verdure green, making splendid pas- ture for the cattle, and cooling the earth after three months of sunshine. _

The town of Salem is the capital of the State, and contains some noble buildings, a State House, and Court House and largo University. The streets are lighted by electric light, and are not less than 60 feet wide, with wood side walks, and tram lines. , It is situated on the bank of the Willamette river, from which the valley takes its name. It is one of the most fertile valleys in the United States, being sheltered by three ranges of mountains—the Cascade, the Coast, and the Blue mountains. The average elevation of these ranges is 5,000 feet. Mount Hood and Mount Jefferson, in the Cascades, being covered' with perpetual snow form a grand picture from any part of the valley, which is sixty miles across. The land is slightly rolling, sometimes covered with stunted oak or brushwood, and at others covered with cedar or firs, some of which are 200 feet high and 20 feet in circum.. femme. Then there are miles of prairie land on which there have never been any trees. The value of the land ranges from 15 dollars to 350 dollars per acre, according to the improvements. The products are wheat, oats, barley, flax, peas, and all sorts of vegetables, second to none in the world ; but it is sea fruit-growing country that , the Willamette Valley is destined to takt the first , rank. Apples, pears, prunes, cherries, and peaches : grow to an unusual size, and are of the finest flavour.! and the trees are literally broken with their load of luscious fruit. Berries, such as raspberries and strawberries, are very prolific. Blackberries are hero cultivated they are much larger, and the trees yield more than they do in England. Veg.:- tables ;pow to an enormous size with very little cultivation. On the next farm to my home the farmer dug up a parsnip over three feet long. Ile had single potatoes weighing nearly 51bs. Ile also gathered 350 bushels from an acre.after ploughing, a goodly number being left in the ground. They do not dig up the potatoes here ; they just plough them out. Cucumbers and tomatoes grow out in the Held pumpkins, squash, and melons are in great variety, some being 50Ibs. weight, and of splendid flavour. Grapes grow and ripen in large quantities, but do not pay so well as hop-growing, as I am told there is very rarely a failure in Oregon hops. When other places have failed with their hops, Oregon has had a grand harvest. Take the land altogether.this is one of the finest place in the ' world for a man with a small capital to take up farm lands and make a home, and there is room , for thousands of families in this State of Oregon. _ . . .

The people, no I find them, are very sociable and free ; very willing to make your acquaintance. One of the traits of the people is that the workman is equal to his employer, awl addresses him as Tom, , Dick, or Derry, just as be does Ida slinpmates. The gentlemen as. rule do not dress as smartly as they do in the old country, but the ladies fully make up, by their excess, for any deficiency on the part of the. gentlemen. . . . . .

The tradesmen here at Salem are nearly all old residents. and are very keen after the "almighty dollar." As a rule they run the workman very hard to get the value out of his labour. Most of them are very conservative in their habits; they do not want any change. They have made a com- petency here, and others must do the same if they I can. There are some who do not want any works I or manufactories to spring up, They are content to boon out their money at tense fifteen per cent. on good security, but lam happy to say there is a race of men coming to the front who are trying to develope to the utmost all the resources of this valuable country, and the old men will have to die off out of the way to make room for the improvements the times require. I find there are a lot of gentlemen connected with the Oregon Land Company who are determined to push along any enterprise that will develope industries. They are the ohms for an emigrant to come in contact with. They will find him a home if he is in search of one, and I am sure they will treat him well. I wish them every SUCCO49 in their endeavour to get the State tilled up with thriving homesteads. There ion strong tide of emigrants from the Eastern States coming here who make good farmers, and will soon till up the vacant lands. There is another class of emigrants I would like to call your attention to—that is the Chinese. In my opinion it is a kind of slave traffic. A" boos" Chinaman goes over to China and brings back a lot of his countrymen for whom he enters into an agreement with his Government to return either their bodies or their hones, he paying all expenses, and finding them with food and hiring them out to labour. Thus, if ,they live, they, work out their
Freedom, and I tell you they do hare to work, either in the laundry or in cutting wood ; they litorally work like alaves. _ _

The average rate of wages for joiners is IN dollars per week of 60 hours. Everybody gets fairly paid. The barbers charge 25 cents. or Is. Ohl. for cutting hair, and 10 cents. for shaving. If some of the Warrington artists could obtain that price, I guess they would soon be in a position to quit the business. The blacksmith charges two dollars or 85.4,1. for shoeing one horse. Crockery ware is very dear, and of very inferior quality. Butchers' meat is very cheap, the best joints being only 10 cents. or 51. per lb. Sugar is rattier dearer than in England, being 7 cents per lb. And now I sir 1 conclude, as my letter may become weari- some.— Yours sincerely,

rho CH .M. fst said that, as, since they last met, their Clerk had been elected the first county councillor for Winwiek division, he thought it vrould hen good thing if they pawed a resolution congratulating him on the fact. Ile was sure they were all very glad to see him in the honourable position, and the general feeling of the Board was that Mr. Sutton as a efounty couneillor was a square man in a square hole—he was the right man in the right ' place. Ilear, hear.) lie would move that the Guardians express their hearty congratulations to their clerk on his election no the first county councillor of the Winwick division of Lancashire.—Mr. tingsvito, in seconding the proposal, said he did not think thee could have a tuan on the Counts. As a Board of Guardians they had no right a! all to meddle with Mr. Sutton's private affairs.—Mr. tinrts- suns, interrupting, said be could not sit there and listen to all that nonsense. He really must protest against Mr. Ratcliffe getting up and making all those remarks. It was not fair that their time should be taken up in that way, and he begged to move that Mr. Ratcliffe either keep Ins seat, or speak with some sort of sense that they could understand, or else go out of the rooon.—Mr. Rat-- Mr. You are only one member. There is no Jr. business about this.—Mr. Joiner said it would ben credit and not a disgvace to that Boartl to pass such a resolution as had been proposed, and he was sorry for the remarks that had been made. Ile was sure they woai,l gain rather than Ifte by Mr. Sutton's election—Mr. Rawls see I don't say anything to Ithe contrary—Tine Chairman You have spoken already, Mr. Ratcliffe.—Mr. Dsarsvtasrrn did not see any objec- tion to the proposition, especially as the Chairman was an elector of the Winwick division. lie, howevw, did not see that the Board had au:Nothing to de with it except through the ratepayers of the Winwick division.—Mr. Jl3l.l.ltir The Guardians are not to he tongue-tied.— Mr. IlaninsoN must say that the Chairman had rather taken him by surprise in moving the resolution. He was not quite mare whether the Clerk's position as a County Councillor might not, to some extent, affect his pertition as Clerk to the Board. If he could be sure on that point, he would have no difficulty in supporting the rert oIu- tion.—Mr.W.HOVIIIITON supported the resolution for the reason that the Clerk, by virtue of his office as clerk, was exactly the man they wanted for the position he had attained.—The CLAna said that if the resolution could have had the slightest effect on the deetions he should have opposed is at once, but this it could not lase. When he was elected to that Board he was a member of the borough Town Council and he could have' continued a member of that body if he had chosen Now he had simply taken an office whidi might bed a, somewhat higher character than being a member of the Councilof a small boroughbut his position in that respect was n:t changed. div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Town Ha on Tuesday. Mr. T. Sutton Timmis J.P., presided,and there were present the Very Rev. Dean Finegan, Rev. Father Clarke, Dr. O'Keeffe, Major Wareing, Messrs. 11. Wade Deacon, it'., F. Reyes, and G. 11. Danby (clerk). I DISTRICT EDUCATION. _.. - .

The District id-t-n;iivo-n--JiilWinift.ce reported that during December (three weeks) there were 66 applies- ' tions for payment of school fees, whirl) were recommen- ded to be paid in 64 cases. There were 166 persons summoned before the Committee for contravention of the Education As-f; 18 were prosecuted before the magistrates, and 17 convicted snd fined. The Atten- dance Officer (P. J. Rowe), having completed six years service, it was resolved that his salary be increased £3 per annum. according to the scale of the Board.—The minutes were passed.
THE INDUSTRIAL SCHOOLS ACT.

.—,.-.....—.. The District Education Committee recommended that ' the following petition he adopted, and that the same be ! signed by the Chairman on behalf of the Board, and forwarded to the Right Honourable Henry Matthews. QC , M.P., WM. Principal Secretary of State for the Home Department That your memorialists, the School Board for the district of Widnes, have Once their formation in 1874, carried cad the powers invested in School Boards, by Sections 27 and 28, of the Elementary F.dueation Act, 1870 That 93 children have been sent from the district of Widnes to Industrial Schools, and that 39 are at present in such schools. That no child has for many years been sent to an Industrial School by the magistrates of this division, until thorough enquiry hon been made into theca. by your memorialists. 'Gat by a Committee of the Board, and the use of three attendance officers, your memorialists have excellent means of inquiring into the cases of neglected. vagrant. and incomgeble children. That a Bill waa Introduced into the Howe of Lords by DIA Brownlow, in August last, entitled, " An Act to Consolidate and amend the Acts relating to Industrial Schools in Groat Britain," whereby inter al is it was provided that the power now possessed by School Boards, to contribute towards the inaintenanceof children in Industrial Schools,should cease That your memorialists apprehending that a Bill con- taining similar provisions may be again introduced, respectfully urge that the existing powers should still be vested in School Boards, and that the transference of the power to the Guardians would be prejudicial to, and seriously interfere with, the work which your mem- orialists have been carrying out. That your memorial- ists would be hindered in carrying into effect the law compelling the attendance of children at whoa. seeing that it is impossible to 'continually pr.ecute parents who have incorrigible children, or who are too poor to pay the fines, and who have in consequence t go to prison. That Tr.nt Schools are of .e only in eases where the home influences brought to bear on the children are at least fairly decent, and that the power reserved to School Boards to :erect, and maintain. day Industrial Schools is useless to all boards of compara- tively small or scattered districts, sot. coot of erection and maintenance, and the difficulty of compelling the attendance of the children would be too great. Your memorialists therefore pray, that their memorial may receive your consideration, and that amendments may be inserted in se,ordance therewith if the Bill he again intesinced." Mr. Deacon, in moving the .edoption ot the memorial, ex- plained that the subject had arisen upon a petition Does the Manchreter School Board. The Bill referred to in the memorial was based upon the report of a Royal Cotnmis- sion issued in 18733, which showed that the power to rsael children to industrial schools lead been abused. The Committee did not send children to an industrial , school merely for truancy, but because they were on the ! nester line of crime, and the irol.trial school seemed to be the proper Owe for them. trader this proposed new Act there would he no public authority responsible for bringing Use children, before the magistrates, and Um

The first portion of the Moore Sectien in comparison ,svt..h other parts of the worksetill percents an appearance of; inactivity. Nearer to Acton Grange where the ease:t- wat:ma is through rock, a large mapher of inert are emplyved in stone-cutting and blasting. At the "settle- ment at the latter place the mission work is prosecuted with vigour amongst young and old. Resides the usual servicce and a Sunday School for the children, the mud,- tatigabk, missionaries arrange entertaimments, night classes, v. which meet a decided want among the workawn. In walking along the cutting towards Walton the most strWing feature is perhaps the railway embank- mekt which has lately increased considerably and is a constant object of interest amongst passengers ob the: London and North-Western Railway. Nearer to Stockton Heath, careful ',separations are being made near the Chester-,d. for the kenstruction of the luck joining the i Ship Canal with the Runcorn and Latchford Canal. The I steam navvies at the extreme end of the cutting are being! removed to other parts, some being employed close to ! in widening the main couras of the Canal, and it is evi- dent that the small excavation joining the two water way, will be made by hand-lab sir. The weather has lately been most favourable for work and appears to have been taken full advantage of.

div.head: EMPLOYER LIAMLITY
div.p: THE EMPLOYER LIAMLITY

At Runcorn County Court, on Tuesday, flier; was net down for hearing by His Honour Judge Ffoulkos and a common jury, a case in which Martha Pyke, of 28. Cartwright-at., widow, sought to recover from Mr. T. A. Walker, contractor to the Ship Canal, £3OO damages for the death of her husband. The action was brought under the Employers' Liability Act. Mr. J. P. Cart- wright, of Cheater, wan for the plaint,ff, and the defen- dant was represented by Mr. J. M. Yates, barrister (instructed by Messrs. Perks, Watkin, Heald, and Co., of Manchester. On the 6th August a train of wagons were standing on the metals at the Big Field, Norton, and the deceased was engaged in attach- , ing an 5 link to the coupling of one of the wagons, when ho wan crushed between the buffers. He expired next day. Before the jury was sworn the parties to the action had. conference, with the result that Mr. Yates announced to His Honour that a settlement had been arrived at, it having been agreed that a verdict fox £ll5 and taxed ~outs ihould he entered. Mr: Yates addecl that Hr. Walker did not admit any liability in this action, list he 'WM very liberal to his men, and as the deceased met his death in his service, he desired to act in a generous spirit. The jury was then dis- charged.

div.head: PARNELL INQUIRY.
div.p: THE PARNELL INQUIRY.

When the Parnell Commission resumed its sittings on; Tuesday the court 3Vas crowded. Sir Charles Ruseell ' applied for an order against the proprietor of the ! "Worcester Daily Times and Journal," on account of an 1 article which was alleged to comtitute contempt of 1 court, and the President said they would dual with the matter later on. The Attorney-General then called attention to an article in "United Ireland," commenting on the proceedings. Mr. Wm. O'Brien, M.P., editor of that newspaper, was in court, and he made a long speech, with a view of showing that the publication of the article in question did not constitute an act of con- tempt. The President mid the court would reserve their judgment. Mr. Brodriek, Warden of Merton, next appeared in reference to a speech made by him at Oxford, and said he never meant his words to convey the interpretation spat upon them, and the Court accepted Mr. Brodnek's explanation. The court next heard the evidence of Major Tanner (brother of Dr. Tanner, M.P.), a land agent in Tipperary, who spoke of the difficulty of collecting rents after tho establishment of the Land League. Com-examined by Mr. Michael Devitt, witness mid he did not refuse to go into the house to see his dead mother because Or. Tanner was there. Ile did not go into the some room. He regretted that the name had been mentioned, as he could have given very serious evidence. A witness named lege next gave evidence, and the court adjourned. On Wednesday the president gave judgment in Mr. W. O'Brien's case of alleged contempt of,court. He mid emphatically that the Commissioner had nothing to do with political quustions. Ihe Court...cent.' Mr. O'Brien's statement that he did not desire to my anything disrespectful of the Court, and they would remit any! punishment, with a caution as to the future. The principal witness for the day was Patrick Delaney, who was associated with the Fenian tnovetnent, and who was now brought from 9laryborough Prison, Queen's County. He was examined at some length as to the operations of a Fenianorganisation several years ago. tie statedthat he had been told off to murder Mr. FoNter' and that Earl Spencer wm among those tote murdered. On Thursday Patrick Delany, the t' Invincible," was recalled and cross-examined by Mr. If Old. Ile mid he was certain that Itoyton gave Brady, who was executed, an order in the suininer of 1882, Boyton pointing Mr. Burke out to Brady am: telling him that that was the man. Mr. Devitt next questioned the witness no to his (Mr. Devitt's) own movements. The witness mid that noon after Mr. Davitt's release in 1878 he attended a secret meeting of Fenlans. He never knew of Mr. Devitt being attacked for leaving the Fenian organisation. The wi nese further stated that he had seen Mr. Devitt with Dan Curley in Dublin in 1881. Witnma recognised the photograph of a man called t' No. 1" put in by the Attorney General. The President ordered the witams to be detained in London. Mr. Reginald Digby, agent to Lord Digby, who owns estates in King's C.tinty, spoko of tenants paying their rent in secret after 1879, no they said they were afraid tom openly. Mr. George Ilewson, agent for properties in several counties in Ireland, gave similar evidence. The Attorney General produced a correspondence between Mestere. Matthew Harris, John Dillon, and T. Brennan, ranging from 1877 to 1880, and relating to the agitation. After an arrangement had been made between the Prmident and counsel for facili- tating the inquiry in reference to the alleged Parnell letters, the Court adjourned. Yesterday, the Attorney-General intiinattal that lie would not give evidenee regarding the Plan of Campaign as an independent branelL—Gemege Young, son of a landowner of Donegal, was recalled and examined by Mr. Murphy sate the intimidation of tenants online estate.—Mr. Garrett-Tyrrell, a land and estate agent, said Inc resided in King's County. People who had offended had their hay burned and sheep maimed—Mr. Robert Wood, another agent, gave similar evidence affecting county Mayo. 1

With difficulty she managed to escape from hill] and ran out of the house. On returning shortly after- wards, in company with a loan and a female neighbour, she found her husband lying dead on a bed in the front bedroom, having cut Ina throat. In support of the candidature of Mr. IL Linaker a meeting ol ratepayers was heist in the Church Schoolroom on Tuesday evening. Mr. E. Aaron presides! and there was a representative gathering of ratepayera. The Climaxes, in introducing the candidate said he had known hisn on and off for the Lost 28 or 27 years. During all the time that he had met him at the Runcorn Board if (ivardians) and ut Daresbury Highway Board he could conscientiously say that he had always found him ready and willing to keep down expenses and reduce rates. !applause.) Mr. Lmaker, who was received with applause, said Ire woo thereon a candidate for the County Council, not for any glorifieation of himself, or at his own desire. He was requeot.l in the first instance to come forward for the Foodahans divrtion, where he lived, but he declined absolutely. He woo then waited upon by a candidate who had been selected by the Farmers' Club in Warring- ton, and he a deputation of representative ratepayers who requeked him to cosne forward for the Daresbery. division. He declined, although be was compelled to admit that from hi, knowledge of local and county affairs he might be of some use, if he became a member of the Council. rlsey came a second time, and ulti- mately prevailed upon him to issue an address (Applauass.) The County Council would have to deal with the main roads of the county. At present there were snout 580 miles of main roasts which were kept in repair by the scvmd Highway Boards. The County Council would take over the whole of the expense of the main roam, and the probability was that they would contract with the seders,' Highway Boards in the county to maintain the part of the main reads that were in their several districts. On the County Council Nino formed they would take up the adminintrative busineas of the justices in quarter wantons and, to enable them to do the work, the whole of the officers of the county—the clerk of the peace, the treasurer, the surveyor, &c.—would he passed over to .he County Council, and they would have •Psprowide their salarirt. The county auditor would not I'be required. In future the Government district auditor I would audit the whole of the accounta, and if he found ' any payments wrongly charged to the Council he had tswer to disallow it. and charge thone who had signed the cheque for it. Afterwards, as vacancies occurred, the Council would appoint its own official, with the exception of the clerk of the peace, who woold be appointed by the joint Committee of magistrates and ) councillors, which would he formed for the management of the pollee. The County Council would always have to take over the maintenance of the lunatic asyl s, the sesnion•hOUSea, the police stet inrie aml magistrates rooms, and in Cheshire there were something like 80 of thrte magistrate,' rooms and session hones. The Council would have to maintain the whole of the county bridges, of which there were about 300 in Cheshire : so that they would see the Council would have something to do. The Council WOUla aka have to appoint the county coroners. The Council might abolish any of those offices he had earned, but it they did abolish them they would hovels notpennate the person whose office they took away for the tow he might sustain by the abolition of that office. Then means would have to be provided for the carrying out at those vomits, for the maintenance of buildingn and reads and neon; and in addition to the county rate which moult have to be levied, the Council would have the thee on all intoxicating liquors, the pMeeedS of thongs, 'from beer retailers, apint dealers, sweet dealers, wine dealers., refreshment-house keepers, dogs, gam., appraisers, auctioneers, tobacco dealert, and licenses for carriages, trade carts, locomotives, horses, horse dealers, arinoVial hearings, male servants, hawkers, pawnbrokers, and plate deals.o. The proceeds of those licenses would be credited by the Exchequer to the County Council, instead of guing to the Government an they did now, and also all penalties in respect of suds matters, and also four-fifths of ono-half of the probate duties,more commonly know nun the death dotter. The van and wheel tax was intended to have been added to all those things, but as they were aware, that tax was abandoned by Government. He was rather sorry that it was abandoned, because he thought there were many vans, RagOSIS, and carts that cut up their road, that slid not pay a sufficient sum to the maintenance of those roads. (Applause.! The County Council would take over the regulation.) with respec to the Cattle Dimas. Act. There were some farmers who had suffered moat frightfully from the regulations) of that Set. He thought these regulations were most detrimental to the interests of the fanners, and they required to be eutsiderably amended. There had been some dirty things thrown out about the Awe.sment Committee of the Runcorn Union, and particularly about the Chairman of that Committee, to the effect that the Committee had not done their duty. Now whore, made a remark of that kind did not know what Inc was talking about. He would give them a few simple fact,. In 1885 the property ot the Weaver times!) the Runcorn and Northwich Unions was not rated stall; neither the 4.1r.5, warehouses, canal, or anything else tolonging to the trustee, had paid any- thing at all. TERRIBLE COLLIERY EXPLOSION AT
Y DE. TWENTY-FIVE LIVES LOST. . _

_ Yesterday morning, shortly after nine o'clock, • terrible explosion occurred at the Hyde Colliery of Messrs. .1. W. Sidebotham and Brothers, by which it is feared a large number of men have beim killed. The explosion occurred about one mile from the pits mouth. The men work with lamps and naked lights. it is supposed a lump of rock fell and, releasing gas. sensed the explosion. Between eighty and one hundred colliers are employed regularly at this pit, but a larger number Were employed on Friday owing to drafts from another colliery being introduced. A number of injured men, and the bodies of Seven who were %found dead after the explosion, had been brought to the pit mouth at two o'clock, but it is supposed there were eighteen others in the vicinity of the explosion, none of whom could have escaped _ .

(Applause.) The agricultural industry was as large as any three commercial businesses, and tanners should have a voice in the management of their county affairs. With regard to the Contagious Dimases (Animals) Act, wh,ieh very- closely affected farmers, Mr. Knowles was of opinion that rime alterations should be made in the removal regulations, and that the cost of all animals slaughtered under the provisions of the Act should be borne by the Imperial Exchequer. The question of licensing. he thought, was one for the ' ratepayers to deal with. He had been described as the nominee of a clique, and as the member of a clique. He was a member of the clique that paid the rates. (Applause.) If he was returned, he should go to the council prepared to act fearlessly, uncontrolled by any considerations other than the desire to watch their interests to the best of his ability. (Applause.)—Mr. John Mclntrye proposed That this meeting is or opinion that Mr. Joseph Knowles is a fit and proper person to represent the Appleton Division of this county on the County Council:' In Mr. Know-I.B° said, they had a capital candidate, who had always been found on the side of efficieuey,cutubined with economy. —The proposition was seconded by Mr. Joseph Smith, who, referring to the need of farmers to secure repre- sentation of their views, mid that they had been taxed until the land alino4 groaned under the weight. (Applause.)—Mr. Vrilliain Hout,th supported the resolu- tion which was put to the meeting and carried with a few dissentients.—Mr. R. 11. Kerr then-upon said that it was Ilk intention to prop's° an amettd- moot.— The Chairman : Vita have come here to upset the meeting. and lam determined you shall not °wet it, so si down.—Mr. Kerr mid that it was not his intention. There was no One for whom he had a greater respect than Mr. Knowles.—The Chairman , You will keep your seat—Mr. Kerr I will metre an amend- ment to tins resolution.—After a little further altercation Mr. Kerr proposed, man amendment that Mr. Knowles was not a At and proper person to represent the division on the Counts- Council.—The atnendment was seconded by Mr. Joseph Cooper, but on a vote being taken, only about a desen hands were held up in favour of it. The meeting was then concluded by the loaning of a vote of thanks to the chairman.
